summary: Lists the numbers assigned for networks, protocols and similar identifiers used on the ARPA Internet at the time. It was one edition in a series of such lists. This RFC is historic. Replaced by RFC 790.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 776 is a snapshot of number assignments used by network protocols in January 1981. It lists values for networks, IP versions, protocols, ports or sockets, and links.

questions: which protocol number did the list give tcp and udp
subtitle: A January 1981 list of assigned network, protocol, port, and link numbers.

tldr.problem: Network protocol implementations needed coordinated assignments for numbers identifying networks, protocols, ports, sockets, and links.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC publishes the current assigned values and says the list will be updated periodically, with assignments handled by Jon Postel.

sections.title: Purpose of the Assigned Numbers List
sections.content:
The RFC documents assigned values from several number series used in network protocol implementations. It says the document will be updated periodically and that current information and new assignments could be obtained from Jon Postel.

The listed categories include network numbers, Internet version numbers, Internet protocol numbers, port or socket numbers, and link numbers. The RFC identifies the responsible person or a reference for listed items.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocols use numbers to identify networks, services, and other items. This document records the assignments and explains how to request a new one.

sections.title: Network, Version, and Protocol Numbers
sections.content:
The network-number list uses an 8-bit field. The Internet version number field is 4 bits, with version 4 assigned to Internet Protocol and version 5 to ST Datagram Mode. The IP Protocol field is 8 bits and identifies the next-level protocol.

The list assigns protocol number 6 to TCP and 17 to User Datagram Protocol. It includes other assigned, reserved, and unassigned values in the same tables.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists separate numbers for networks, IP versions, and protocols carried by IP. For example, its table assigns 6 to TCP and 17 to UDP.

sections.title: Ports, Sockets, and Links
sections.content:
The port or socket table explains that ports in TCP and sockets in AHHP identify ends of logical connections. Assigned port and socket values use the low-order 8 bits, with the other bits cleared to zero. Ranges distinguish network-wide standard functions, host-specific functions, reserved values, and experimental functions.

The link-number section describes a field in the ARPANET Host/IMP interface leader. It explains that the field had changed into the high-order 8 bits of a 12-bit message-ID field, with the low-order 4 bits normally zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The tables also assign numbers to connection endpoints and Host/IMP links. They divide values into standard, host-specific, reserved, and experimental groups.
